questions.statement: What can be inferred from the text?
questions.context: Text: The clinic opened at six in the morning and by eight all the appointments for the day were already taken. Staff now arrive before six to prepare the rooms.

options.text: Demand for appointments is higher than the clinic originally expected
options.feedback: Full bookings by eight and an earlier start for staff show demand beyond what the clinic planned for.

options.text: The clinic intends to close earlier in the afternoon
options.feedback: Nothing in the text mentions afternoon closing times.

options.text: Most patients prefer afternoon appointments
options.feedback: The appointments fill before midday, so the text supports the opposite of an afternoon preference.

options.text: The clinic has plans to hire more doctors
options.feedback: No hiring plan appears anywhere in the passage.

questions.explanation:
An inference is a conclusion the reader draws by combining facts that the text states separately. Here the early fill-up and the earlier staff arrival both point to the same unstated cause.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What is the most likely explanation for the cracks?
questions.context: Text: Last year the road was repaired for the first time in twenty years. This year the surface has developed cracks in exactly the places where the heavy machinery was used.

options.text: The machinery used during the repair damaged the new surface
options.feedback: The location of the cracks matches where the machinery worked, so the repair itself is implicated.

options.text: The road was never repaired at all
options.feedback: The text states plainly that the road was repaired last year.

options.text: The cracks are caused by heavy rain only
options.feedback: Rain is not mentioned, and the coincidence of location points to another cause.

options.text: The road was repaired twice in the same year
options.feedback: Only one repair is reported, so no second repair can explain the damage.

questions.explanation:
Inferences drawn from position are often the strongest available: if a defect appears exactly where something was done, that something is a plausible cause even without an explicit statement.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What does the comparison allow the reader to conclude?
questions.context: Text: Two schools joined the recycling programme. In the first, the bins were placed in every classroom and participation rose by half. In the second, the bins stayed in the central yard and participation did not change.

options.text: Where the bins were placed mattered more than whether the school joined
options.feedback: Both schools joined the same programme, so the only stated difference is the placement of the bins.

options.text: The second school has less motivated students
options.feedback: Student motivation is never mentioned in the text.

options.text: Recycling programmes never work in schools
options.feedback: The first school shows a clear improvement, which contradicts a general claim that programmes never work.

options.text: Central yards attract more rubbish
options.feedback: No claim about rubbish or the yard itself appears in the text.

questions.explanation:
When two cases are compared and only one variable differs, the conclusion about that variable is the strongest inference available. The comparison in this text is designed to make exactly one factor visible.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which statement does the text leave open?
questions.context: Text: The number of visitors to the museum doubled in three years, while the museum's own staff grew by only two people.

options.text: How the museum managed to serve twice as many people
options.feedback: The text gives the two figures but never explains the mechanism, so that question remains unanswered.

options.text: Whether the number of visitors rose at all
options.feedback: The doubling is stated explicitly, so that question is closed.

options.text: Whether the staff were paid more
options.feedback: No information about salaries appears, and the question of payment is outside what the text covers.

options.text: Whether the museum changed its opening hours
options.feedback: Opening hours are never mentioned, so no conclusion can be drawn from the passage.

questions.explanation:
A well-constructed comprehension question asks about what the text does not settle. Recognising the boundary of a passage is as important as retrieving what it states.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What does this change in customer behaviour suggest?
questions.context: Text: After the ban on plastic bags, checkout staff reported that many customers now refuse the thin bags offered at the till and ask for paper ones instead.

options.text: The ban influenced habits at the point of purchase, not only in policy
options.feedback: The refusal happens at the till, which shows the policy reaching actual consumer decisions.

options.text: Customers no longer buy anything in plastic
options.feedback: Refusing thin bags is not the same as abandoning plastic entirely.

options.text: Paper bags are cheaper for the shop
options.feedback: No price comparison between materials appears in the text.

options.text: The ban was withdrawn shortly afterwards
options.feedback: The text reports an effect of the ban and gives no sign that it was withdrawn.

questions.explanation:
Behavioural evidence is strong evidence that a policy works. A report about what people actually do at the counter carries more weight for a reader than a statement about what the law permits.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What does the detail about the areas not exposed to rain imply?
questions.context: Text: The station was repainted last winter. Passengers who use it daily say the paint has begun to peel in areas that are not exposed to rain.

options.text: Weather is not the cause of the peeling
options.feedback: If peeling occurs where there is no rain, the weather cannot explain it.

options.text: The paint is of a very good quality
options.feedback: Peeling within months is evidence of poor performance, not of good quality.

options.text: The station is used mostly in the rainy season
options.feedback: The description of areas without rain says nothing about when passengers travel.

options.text: The station needs to be repainted every winter
options.feedback: Nothing in the text supports a yearly repainting schedule.

questions.explanation:
A detail can be informative because of what it rules out. The reader who notices that the damaged areas are sheltered uses that absence to eliminate a whole category of explanation.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What is the most reasonable inference about those four species?
questions.context: Text: Volunteers counted birds in the reserve for five years. Four species that had been common every year disappeared after the second year and have not returned.

options.text: Something in the reserve changed in a way that affected them
options.feedback: A sudden disappearance after a stable period points to a change in conditions that those species could not tolerate.

options.text: The counting method was wrong in the second year
options.feedback: The continued counting would have revealed a counting error, and the text reports a consistent result.

options.text: Those species migrated permanently to another continent
options.feedback: Permanent migration to another continent is possible in principle but nothing in the text supports it.

options.text: They were never present in the reserve
options.feedback: They were recorded as common in the first two years, so they were certainly present.

questions.explanation:
Inference questions often hinge on a change in a pattern. A stable period followed by sudden absence suggests a cause in the environment rather than in the observation.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which conclusion is justified by the text?
questions.context: Text: The factory cut its water use by a third. The same period saw the arrival of a new washing machine that uses less water per load.

options.text: Part of the reduction may be attributable to the new equipment
options.feedback: The new machine is one identified factor, and the text gives no reason to exclude it from the reduction.

options.text: The new machine alone explains the entire reduction
options.feedback: One machine cannot plausibly account for a reduction of a third across the whole factory.

options.text: The reduction was caused by a fall in production
options.feedback: No fall in production is mentioned anywhere in the passage.

options.text: The old machines were replaced by hand washing
options.feedback: Hand washing is not suggested by any sentence in the text.

questions.explanation:
Careful inference limits itself to what the text supports and uses cautious wording for partial explanations. Claiming a total or exclusive cause would go beyond the evidence given.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Why do the researchers mention what they did not measure?
questions.context: Text: A survey found that students who sleep less than six hours score lower on attention tests. The researchers add that they did not measure how long each student had been awake before the test.

options.text: To flag a limitation that weakens the interpretation of the correlation
options.feedback: Naming an uncontrolled variable signals that the correlation may not reflect a direct relationship.

options.text: To show that the study was technically advanced
options.feedback: Stating a limitation is the opposite of advertising technical strength.

options.text: To suggest that attention tests are unreliable
options.feedback: The comment concerns time awake, and nothing suggests that the tests themselves were unreliable.

options.text: To explain why the sample was small
options.feedback: No information about the size of the sample appears in the text.

questions.explanation:
A limitation statement is a form of intellectual honesty that advanced readers look for. It tells the reader exactly where the evidence stops and the interpretation should stop with it.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Why does one article give the reader an advantage over the other?
questions.context: Text: Two newspapers reported the same figures from the ministry. Only one of them also included the figure for the previous year, which allowed its readers to see that the number had fallen.

options.text: It supplies the comparison that makes the trend visible
options.feedback: A current figure means little without the earlier one, so the comparison is what creates understanding.

options.text: It reports a different ministry
options.feedback: Both articles come from the same ministry, so the source is identical.

options.text: It uses a shorter headline
options.feedback: Headline style has no bearing on what the reader can learn from the figures.

options.text: It was published earlier in the day
options.feedback: The text says nothing about the order of publication.

questions.explanation:
Data acquire meaning through comparison. This item asks the reader to notice that the difference between two reports is not the information itself but the frame that makes it interpretable.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What problem does this change in method introduce?
questions.context: Text: The study followed the same sixty households in both years. In the first year their electricity use was measured from meter readings; in the second, from a sample of households that volunteered to share readings.

options.text: The two years used different samples, so the results may not be comparable
options.feedback: Comparing two years requires the same subjects, and a smaller voluntary sample breaks the continuity.

options.text: The first year measured more households than the second
options.feedback: The second year covers fewer households, so the first did not measure more.

options.text: Meter readings are known to be inaccurate in the second year
options.feedback: The concern is about comparability, not about the accuracy of any particular meter.

options.text: The households that volunteered used more electricity than the others
options.feedback: Nothing in the text compares the volunteers with non-volunteers on usage.

questions.explanation:
Methodological detail in a passage is often included precisely so that a reader can spot a threat to validity. Inference questions on research texts often hinge on whether the method supports the comparison the authors draw.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What warning does the passage imply?
questions.context: Text: A guide to the trail advises hikers to carry water, since the last village lies six kilometres behind the ridge. Several hikers have treated the spring near the ridge as a refill point.

options.text: The spring cannot be relied upon as a source of water
options.feedback: The advice to carry water plus the hikers who depend on the spring imply that it is unreliable.

options.text: The spring is the best place to refill
options.feedback: Treating the spring as a refill point is presented as a mistake, not a recommendation.

options.text: The trail has no water sources at all
options.feedback: A spring is a water source, so saying the trail has none contradicts the text.

options.text: Hikers should refill only in the last village
options.feedback: Carrying water from the start, not refilling in one village, is what the guide recommends.

questions.explanation:
A passage can imply through juxtaposition: the explicit advice and the reported mistake together build a warning the text never states outright.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which inference is supported by the two sentences together?
questions.context: Text: The notice says the pool will close at six for maintenance. Regular users report that the last lap before six is always crowded.

options.text: Closing time falls just before the period of heaviest use
options.feedback: A crowd in the final session before a six o'clock closing shows that the closing time cuts into the most popular period.

options.text: The pool is rarely used in the evening
options.feedback: A crowded last lap indicates heavy use, which contradicts the claim of little evening use.

options.text: The maintenance work is longer than planned
options.feedback: Nothing in the text says anything about how long the maintenance takes.

options.text: Regular users are unhappy with the pool
options.feedback: The text reports crowding as a fact and expresses no opinion about users' satisfaction.

questions.explanation:
Two sentences from different registers, a notice and an observation, combine into one inference about timing. Joining evidence across sentences is the core skill of inferential reading.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What is the likely reason for the change in the recipe?
questions.context: Text: The recipe calls for two eggs. The version published last month called for three, and reviewers at the time complained that the result was too soft to slice.

options.text: Fewer eggs were used to make the result firm enough to slice
options.feedback: The complaint concerned a result too soft to slice, and reducing eggs is the change that addresses that fault.

options.text: Eggs became more expensive in the shops
options.feedback: Price is never mentioned in the passage.

options.text: The number of reviews dropped after publication
options.feedback: The number of reviewers does not relate to the quantity of eggs.

options.text: The cooking time was shortened in the new version
options.feedback: No change in cooking time appears anywhere in the text.

questions.explanation:
A revision is best explained by the complaint that preceded it. Linking a change in a text to a criticism already recorded is a standard inferential move in informational reading.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What can be inferred about the college's confidence in the change?
questions.context: Text: Attendance at evening classes rose after the college moved the timetable an hour earlier. The college has now applied the same change to the morning programme.

options.text: The result with the first group was favourable enough to extend the change
options.feedback: Extending a change to a second group implies the first produced a satisfactory result.

options.text: The college is testing the change again on the same group
options.feedback: The morning programme is a different group, so the same group is not being retested.

options.text: The evening classes were cancelled after the trial
options.feedback: A rise in attendance is the opposite of a cancellation.

options.text: The timetable change had no measurable effect
options.feedback: An effect was recorded, since attendance rose, which rules out the last reading.

questions.explanation:
Institutional decisions reveal what an organisation believes about its own evidence. An expansion of a programme is a fair signal that the earlier result was judged positive.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What does the writer appear to want the reader to conclude?
questions.context: Text: The writer states that the policy has been in force for three years and that no case has reached the courts. She adds that most disagreements are settled privately before any legal step is needed.

options.text: The absence of court cases does not mean the policy has never caused conflict
options.feedback: By explaining that disputes are settled before any legal step, the writer weakens the inference that no conflict exists.

options.text: The policy has been completely accepted by everyone involved
options.feedback: Settling privately is not the same as universal acceptance, so the conclusion overstates the case.

options.text: The courts have refused to hear cases about the policy
options.feedback: No statement about courts refusing cases appears in the passage.

options.text: Private settlements are legally required by the policy
options.feedback: The text describes what happens, not what the policy legally requires.

questions.explanation:
A writer who qualifies evidence is usually correcting an impression the reader might otherwise form. This item asks the student to identify the implication that the surrounding sentences work to prevent.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Why is this an important point for a critical reader?
questions.context: Text: Two readings of the same chart were possible. One took the vertical axis as the number of households; the other took it as the number of people, and each produces a different claim about average size.

options.text: The same numerical evidence supports different conclusions depending on how it is read
options.feedback: The item shows that interpretation, not just calculation, determines what the evidence means.

options.text: The chart contains an arithmetic error
options.feedback: The problem is the labelling of the axis, and no arithmetic error is mentioned.

options.text: The second reading of the axis is mathematically impossible
options.feedback: Both readings are possible, so the second is not impossible.

options.text: Charts should never be used to support claims about households
options.feedback: The passage shows charts being used appropriately, and the issue is interpretation rather than suitability.

questions.explanation:
Critical reading extends to the conventions behind a source. This item asks the student to notice that a figure can support a claim or its opposite depending on an unstated definition.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: What does the absence of explanation tell the reader?
questions.context: Text: The text describes a decline in the industry and then states that exports in the region rose over the same period. It never explains how both can be true.

options.text: The two trends probably refer to different measures of the industry
options.feedback: Where a text reports two apparently opposite trends without reconciling them, the reader should suspect different underlying measures.

options.text: One of the two statements must be false
options.feedback: Rejecting one statement as false is a conclusion the evidence does not force.

options.text: The author forgot to include a conclusion
options.feedback: An unexplained tension is a feature of the passage rather than proof of carelessness.

options.text: Exports are unrelated to the industry
options.feedback: The connection between the two is exactly what the missing explanation would clarify.

questions.explanation:
When a passage holds two facts together without connecting them, a careful reader does not panic but also does not invent a contradiction. Instead, the gap points to a definitional difference the text never states.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Why does the omission matter for a critical reader?
questions.context: Text: A company announced a new recycling plant. Its report lists the recycling figures and the reduction in costs, but it never mentions that the plant stands on land used for farming until 2019.

options.text: The report presents only the benefits and hides a cost that bears on the decision
options.feedback: A report that lists gains without mentioning a documented loss is selective, and that changes how much weight its figures deserve.

options.text: The report is too short to be credible
options.feedback: Length is not the criterion for credibility, and the report may simply be brief.

options.text: Farming has no economic value in the region
options.feedback: The text does not assess the economic value of farming.

options.text: The plant will certainly increase production
options.feedback: Nothing in the passage establishes any increase in production.

questions.explanation:
Silence in a source is evidence. A reading that notices which relevant fact has been left out evaluates a text more effectively than one that only collects what it states.
---
questions.subject: ingles

questions.statement: Which criticism of the argument is most accurate?
questions.context: Text: A commentator argues that the reform will reduce inequality. Her evidence is that average incomes in the two poorest districts rose after the reform, while the national average remained unchanged.

options.text: A rise in the poorest districts alongside a flat national average may conceal a fall elsewhere
options.feedback: If some incomes rise while the average holds steady, the remaining households must have seen a reduction, which is what the argument leaves out.

options.text: The poorest districts show a fall in income
options.feedback: The text states the opposite for those two districts.

options.text: A national average is never a useful measure
options.feedback: The national average is precisely what the argument uses as its reference point.

options.text: The reform clearly reduced inequality
options.feedback: A flat national average with gains concentrated in two districts does not demonstrate a general reduction.

questions.explanation: Statistical reasoning is part of critical reading. This item asks the student to see that an average can stay constant while its components move in opposite directions.
questions.subject: ingles
